title: Crypto Markets and Decentralised Finance
answer: Exchange routing, yield strategies, on-chain forensics, stablecoin stress and governance tokens.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
children.blurb: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of splitting or sequencing a trade across several on chain liquidity pools rather than sending it to one.

children.name: Yield Strategies in Smart Contracts
children.blurb: Yield strategies in smart contracts cover the ways holders of digital assets try to earn a return by placing those assets into on chain programs rather than leaving them idle.

children.name: On-Chain Forensics
children.blurb: On-chain forensics is the practice of reconstructing what happened on a public blockchain by reading its transaction record.

children.name: Stablecoin Stress Testing
children.blurb: Stablecoin stress testing is the practice of modelling how a token pegged to a fiat currency behaves when redemption pressure, market dislocation or reserve doubts hit at once.

children.name: Governance Token Outcomes
children.blurb: Governance token outcomes covers what happens after a crypto project issues a token that carries voting rights over its protocol, treasury or parameter changes.

sections.body: Crypto markets run on public ledgers, and artificial intelligence is now used to read those ledgers and act on them. In exchange routing, models compare prices and fees across automated market makers to split an order into pieces that fill at better average rates. In yield strategies, agents watch lending rates and liquidity pools and move funds between smart contracts when the expected return changes. On-chain forensics uses clustering and pattern recognition to group wallet addresses and trace where funds came from and went. Stablecoin stress testing simulates redemption runs and market shocks to see how a peg might behave. Governance token outcomes are studied by modelling how votes, delegation and token holdings interact. None of this replaces the underlying blockchain, it sits on top of it and reads what the chain already records.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Routing is the most mature area, because the problem is well defined and the data is public, though latency and failed transactions still cost money. Yield strategies work in calm markets and break down when gas prices spike or a pool is drained, and backtests often flatter results that live trading does not repeat. On-chain forensics has become genuinely useful for exchanges and investigators, but mixers, bridges and privacy tools limit how far a trail can be followed, and attribution is probabilistic rather than certain. Stablecoin stress testing is harder than it looks because the historical record contains few true runs, so models lean on assumptions about holder behaviour that may not hold. Governance token work is the least settled, since voter turnout is low and outcomes depend on off-chain deals that never appear on the ledger. Across all five areas, the honest limit is the same, the models describe a market that can change faster than the data used to train them.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from mechanics to measurement to governance. Routing Across Automated Market Makers and Yield Strategies in Smart Contracts cover the execution layer, how trades are placed and how capital is allocated, and a reader goes there for the operational side of decentralised finance. On-Chain Forensics and Stablecoin Stress Testing cover the analytical layer, one tracing who moved what and the other testing what happens under pressure, and a reader goes there to understand risk and investigation rather than profit. Governance Token Outcomes sits at the end because it depends on the other four, since voting power, liquidity and trading all shape how a proposal fares. Read together, they form a chain from a single trade to the rules that govern the system the trade happens in.
